narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the model strongly toward predicting failure. Being in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of about 5.8 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker performance in later law school years. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; your third-decile placement falls well below the average of 6.0 for accepted students.

Your LSAT score was the second most influential feature, but it worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. At 37, your score sits almost exactly at the average of accepted students, providing some positive signal that was simply not enough to overcome the academic ranking concerns.

Taken together, the model saw your lower class standings in law school as the dominant reasons for concern. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or pursue additional relevant experience, and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score further. These steps would directly address the factors that most affected this outcome. (218 words)
